claim: The Battle of Saraighat was a mainly naval battle fought in 1671 (mid-March per Wikipedia; exact day unknown) on the Brahmaputra at Guwahati, and the Ahoms won.

claim: Facing the large Mughal boats, Ahom soldiers wavered and began to fall back; Lachit (and the Ahom admiral) were seriously ill, which demoralised the troops.

claim: Though ill, Lachit is said to have risen from his sickbed and taken to the river in a boat himself, and the wavering Ahom boats rallied.

sources.title: Live History India: Lachit Borphukan, Assam's Great General
sources.quote: Lachit who was ill at that time is said to have heroically gotten out of his sickbed

sources.title: The Sentinel (Assam) editorial: Lachit Barphukan, the 'man fort' against the Mughals
sources.quote: Even though Lachit was sick, he got up from his bed and immediately ordered the construction of seven boats.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of Saraighat (map to Bhuyan 1947, J.N. Sarkar 1992, S.L. Baruah 1986)
sources.quote: watched from his sickbed in the gatehouse of Itakhuli fort (paraphrase of fetch summary)

qualification: spoken as 'कहते हैं' — sources tell it as a said-to account and differ on details (seven boats; watched from the sickbed first)
notes: Wikipedia summary: he first watched from his sickbed at Itakhuli. LHI says he rowed his own boat at the enemy. Details differ; qualified in narration.

claim: The Brahmaputra at Saraighat is at its narrowest about 1 km wide, a stretch suited to naval defence.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of Saraighat (map to Bhuyan 1947, J.N. Sarkar 1992, S.L. Baruah 1986)

sources.quote: the Brahmaputra between Kamakhya and Saraighat is the narrowest at Guwahati (search-result summary)

notes: Only one page read; the eSamskriti support is a search snippet. Present tense ('रह जाती है') describes the river today; width varies with season, hence 'करीब'.

claim: The Ahoms used small boats and an improvised bridge of boats to attack the Mughal fleet from the front and the rear at once.

claim: There is no historical document for the popular story that Lachit executed his maternal uncle; it survives as tradition (with the saying 'my uncle is not greater than my country').

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of Saraighat (map to Bhuyan 1947, J.N. Sarkar 1992, S.L. Baruah 1986)
sources.quote: footnote 23: tradition says he executed his uncle at Amingaon; no historical document mentions this incident (paraphrase)

sources.title: VIF India: The Buranjis of Assam
sources.quote: Oral tradition preserves a saying ... based on a real historical incident (search-result summary; partisan, treats it as real)

qualification: spoken as 'मशहूर कहानी', with 'कोई पुराना लिखित सबूत नहीं मिलता' — not 'it is false'
notes: We say evidence is lacking, not that it is false. One-source negative claim (Wikipedia footnote) -> medium.
